History:
• 15 minutes ago patient was stung by a wasp while gardening.  
• Immediately developed shallow breathing, chest tightness, tingling of lips (no throat swelling reported).  
• Notices blotchy rash on body; no previous similar reactions.  
• Concern about whether presentation warrants hospital visit.

Past Medical History:
• Eczema.  
• Drug allergy: Penicillin (reaction not specified).  
• Medications: Keeps oral antihistamine at home for prior aerosinusitis (“dose/route/frequency not documented”).  
• No other chronic illnesses, surgeries, or regular medications reported.

Physical Examination:
• Shallow respirations reported, chest tightness.  
• Tingling of lips without visible swelling (per patient).  
• Blotchy cutaneous rash present.  
• No throat swelling noted.  
• Mental status: Conversational, alert, oriented.  
• No other findings available via video.

Impression:
Suspected early anaphylactic reaction to wasp sting with respiratory involvement.

Management Plan:
• Advised immediate activation of emergency services (call ambulance rather than private transport).  
• Instructed wife to assist patient in taking an oral antihistamine while awaiting EMS.  
• Emphasized need for prompt hospital evaluation for possible anaphylaxis.  
• No other outpatient treatments initiated during call.

Patient Summary:
Mr. Jonathan Irving experienced respiratory difficulty, lip tingling, and a blotchy rash within minutes of a wasp sting, raising concern for evolving anaphylaxis. He was instructed to take an antihistamine and call an ambulance for urgent hospital assessment.

Key Takeaways:
• Call 999/EMS immediately—do not drive yourself.  
• Take an oral antihistamine now while waiting for paramedics.  
• Inform responders of penicillin allergy and timing of wasp sting.

Next Steps:
• Emergency department evaluation and management (possible epinephrine, monitoring).  
• Consider referral to allergy clinic after acute episode for venom immunotherapy counseling.  
• Obtain and carry an epinephrine auto-injector if confirmed insect venom allergy.

Quality checks (document_quality):
• Missing elements: vital signs, full medication list, exact antihistamine details, reaction specifics to penicillin, immunization status.  
• Internal conflicts: none noted.  
• Transcript quality: clear; limited by remote assessment and absence of objective exam data.
